# Mars–Moon Orbital Atlas

A shared 3D atlas for Mars and the Moon, built with React, TypeScript, Vite,
React Three Fiber, and Cesium.

- **Mars:** Nine available GLB models associated with Mars or included as off-world references (`sojourner_rover`, `spirit_and_opportunity_rover`, `viking_lander`, `insight_lander`, `ingenuity_helicopter`, `curiosity_rover`, `perseverance_rover`, `mro_orbiter`, and `dawn_spacecraft`, shown in its flyby context), plus three separately scoped reference spacecraft (`near_shoemaker`, `pioneer_10`, `kepler_space_telescope` under `reference_spacecraft`), orbital actors and satellites (`phobos`, `deimos`, `mars_odyssey`, `maven_orbiter`, and `ares_station`, an ISS proxy), and four IAU/USGS features.
- **Moon:** An illustrative globe and surface imagery/textures, two orbiters (`lro_orbiter`, `apollo_csm`), one verified NASA 3D Resources lander GLB (`apollo_lunar_module`, in static inspection mode), three reference features (`mare_tranquillitatis`, `tycho`, `south_pole_aitken`), and six Apollo equipment records from CSV that remain `unavailable` (with illustrative procedural geometry reconstructions).

chunks.text: The globe, thermal/elevation maps, seeded synthesized terrain grid, and procedural reconstructions support educational visualization. They do not replace MOLA, THEMIS, LOLA, or Diviner measurement datasets; the original measured datasets are explicitly listed as not integrated.

chunks.title: README.md — Run locally
chunks.text:
```powershell
npm install
npm run dev
```

To enable the **RISE assistant** (`/api/chat`, launched from the 3D button at
`public/assets/mascot/rise_plushie.glb` through
`src/scene/mascot/RiseMascot.tsx`), configure the server-side `GROQ_API_KEY`
environment variable in `.env.local` locally or in Vercel Environment
Variables (a local `.env` file is also supported). Do not expose it to the
client with the `VITE_` prefix. The backend
uses the `groq-sdk` chat completions API with `openai/gpt-oss-20b`. It grounds
answers in the locally indexed project knowledge in
`src/config/chatKnowledgeIndex.json` (`npm run build:chat-index`).

Choose Mars or the Moon in the top navigation, follow the suggested journey
(`Guided journey`) or switch to `Explore freely`, use `?v=1&body=...` for shared
links, and view sources and model status in the right-hand information panel.

chunks.title: README.md — Test and build
chunks.text:
```powershell
npm test
npm run typecheck
npm run validate:assets
npm run build
npm run verify:dist
npm run test:browser
```

`validate:assets` inventories all 28 `.glb` files in `public/assets/models/`
(separating 22 catalog/orbital/terrain runtime GLBs from six non-catalog
preload/LOD/legacy GLBs) and one UI mascot `.glb`
(`public/assets/mascot/rise_plushie.glb`), verifying glTF `2.0`, byte counts,
SHA-256, and six terrain-region manifest entries. `verify:dist` compares all
asset files and SHA-256 checksums between `public/` and `dist/` after a build.
`npm run build:chat-index` regenerates the locally sourced knowledge index at
`src/config/chatKnowledgeIndex.json`. `test:browser` runs Playwright/Chrome
with SwiftShader through both Mars and Moon journeys on desktop and narrow
viewports.

Cesium is served from `/cesium/`; GLSL shaders and WASM resources are configured
in Vite. Model assets, textures, audio, and decoders are under `public/assets/`
and `public/decoders/`. Unprocessed source models are under `raw_assets/`.
Data sources and visualization limits are documented in `docs/SOURCES.md`.

chunks.text: # Project Vantalumen - Keeping Space Exploration Stories Alive

chunks.title: VANTALUMEN_INTRODUCTION.md — Summary
chunks.text:
Since the 1960s, NASA has sent many spacecraft and robots to explore the Moon
and Mars. Some are now silent, left behind after completing their missions, but
their stories are far from over. For the "Abandoned but not Forgotten"
challenge, our team created VantaLumen, an interactive educational website that
helps people rediscover these space explorers and the stories behind them.

VantaLumen combines 3D maps of Mars and the Moon, interactive spacecraft
inspections, first-person mission-control-inspired views, and educational
storytelling. It uses NASA open data, including NSSDCA, alongside clearly
identified illustrative visualizations. We believe every spacecraft has a story
worth telling. The machines may be silent, but their stories can still inspire
us.

chunks.title: VANTALUMEN_INTRODUCTION.md — Technologies used
chunks.text:
- **Application:** React 19, TypeScript 5.9, and Vite 7.
- **3D scenes:** Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for interactive 3D
  scenes, model loading, camera controls, and effects.
- **Planetary/geospatial visualization:** Cesium for globe and geospatial
  views; custom GLSL shaders and Three.js terrain rendering for other views.
- **State and animation:** Zustand for shared application state and GSAP for
  camera and interface transitions.
- **Visual and audio effects:** `@react-three/postprocessing` / `postprocessing`
  and Howler.js.
- **Chat assistant:** A server-side API uses Groq's `groq-sdk` with the
  `openai/gpt-oss-20b` model. Its answers are grounded in a locally indexed set
  of project documents and catalog data; `GROQ_API_KEY` is kept server-side.
- **3D asset formats:** glTF/GLB assets, including Draco-compressed models,
  textures, and separate terrain meshes.

- Ingenuity helicopter
- Curiosity rover
- Perseverance rover
- Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO)
- Dawn spacecraft (shown in the context of its 2009 Mars flyby)

Additional spacecraft models available as off-world/reference objects:

- NEAR Shoemaker

- Kepler Space Telescope

- 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter
- MAVEN orbiter

  spacecraft in a current Mars orbit
- Ares Orbital Station concept, using an International Space Station (ISS)

chunks.title: VANTALUMEN_INTRODUCTION.md — What does the website do, and how does it work?
chunks.sourcePath: docs/VANTALUMEN_INTRODUCTION.md#What does the website do, and how does it work?
chunks.section: What does the website do, and how does it work?
chunks.text:
Vantalumen is an interactive educational website that tells the stories of space equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

Our project focuses on real NASA missions, including the Opportunity rover on Mars and the Apollo lunar missions. We want people to learn what happened to these machines, why they were important, and what they can still teach us today.

On our website, users can explore 3D maps of the Moon and Mars and find the locations of different spacecraft. They can also view 3D models of space equipment from different angles. We provide two ways to explore: a normal 3D view and a first-person view inspired by a mission control room.

Another feature shows how space equipment might change over 50 years because of the harsh conditions on the Moon and Mars. We use SVG animations that move as users scroll down the page. This is an educational simulation, not an exact prediction.

We also use information from NASA's official databases, including NSSDCA, to make our stories more accurate and useful.

chunks.title: VANTALUMEN_INTRODUCTION.md — What benefits and intended impacts does it have?
chunks.sourcePath: docs/VANTALUMEN_INTRODUCTION.md#What benefits and intended impacts does it have?
chunks.section: What benefits and intended impacts does it have?
chunks.text:
We created Vantalumen because we believe that space history should be interesting and easy to understand, especially for young people.

For children, we made a comic series about Oppy, a friendly character based on NASA's Opportunity rover. Through Oppy's adventures, children can learn about real events on Mars, such as finding layers of rocks, getting stuck in soft sand, and solving problems during a mission.

We hope these stories will help children become more curious about science and encourage them to ask questions, think creatively, and learn from mistakes.

For older students and adults, our website offers a different way to learn about NASA missions. Instead of only reading articles or looking at photos, they can explore 3D models, learn how the equipment worked, and understand why these missions mattered.

We also want people to think about what happens to space equipment after a mission ends. Even when a rover stops working, it remains part of the history of space exploration.

Through this project, we hope more people will become interested in space science and understand why protecting our space history is important.

chunks.title: VANTALUMEN_INTRODUCTION.md — Creativity and Considerations
chunks.text:
The main idea behind Vantalumen is to tell the stories of machines that can no longer work but still have something important to share.

When we first learned about old rovers and equipment left on the Moon and Mars, we wondered what stories they could tell if they had a voice. This question became the starting point of our project.

We wanted to create something different from a normal information website. That is why we combined 3D exploration, interactive animations, NASA data, and comics in one place.

One of our favorite parts is Oppy's comic series. We use a friendly rover character and simple stories to explain real problems that NASA engineers faced. We believe children can learn difficult science topics more easily when they enjoy the story.

At the same time, we know scientific accuracy matters. We use NASA information for real mission events and make it clear when something is a simulation or an imagined situation.

Our biggest challenge is balancing science, technology, and storytelling. We want the website to be fun, but we also want visitors to learn something real.

For us, Vantalumen is a way to remember the work of past space missions and share their stories with the next generation.

Vantalumen — The mission ends, but the story continues.

- [Jezero, feature 14300](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/14300): 18.41°, 77.69°E.

POIs use the default planetocentric, east-positive coordinate table on each IAU/USGS feature page as reviewed. Alternate control networks/search tables can show different center coordinates; these are approximate feature centers, not landing coordinates. No elevation measurement is attached. The 18 km marker offset is solely a display offset. Scene axes: +Y north, +X longitude 0°, -Z longitude 90°E.

chunks.title: SOURCES.md — Moon facts and coordinates
chunks.text:
- [NASA NSSDCA Moon Fact Sheet](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html), last updated 2024-01-11: mean radius 1737.4 km, sidereal rotation 655.720 hours, mean surface gravity 1.62 m/s², mean orbital velocity 1.022 km/s, diurnal equatorial temperature range 95–390 K, surface pressure 3×10⁻¹⁵ bar. The globe's rotation is an illustrative elapsed-time animation, not a mission clock or ephemeris.
- [Mare Tranquillitatis, feature 3691](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/3691): center 8.35°, 30.83°E; diameter 875.75 km.
- [Tycho, feature 6163](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/6163): center -43.30°, -11.22° (stored as 348.78°E); diameter 85.29 km.
- [NASA Science · The Moon's Largest Basin](https://science.nasa.gov/resource/the-moons-largest-basin/): the published orthographic view is centered 53°S, 191°E. The South Pole–Aitken basin boundary is not defined by the IAU Gazetteer, so this marker is a view center, not an IAU feature center and not a landing coordinate.

The two IAU feature pages give planetographic, east-positive coordinates in the -180°–180° range. The Moon is treated as near-spherical for display, so the catalog stores these centers as east-positive 0°–360° without a planetocentric conversion. These are approximate feature centers; no elevation measurement is attached.

chunks.title: SOURCES.md — Model credits and terms (2/2)
chunks.text:
[NASA media usage guidelines](https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/) include educational/informational 3D media use and require attribution; third-party material has separate terms. Preserve model credits and do not imply endorsement. Sojourner is separately licensed, not a NASA-authored model.

All models use a centered preview with longest dimension normalized to 2 scene units. Original file transforms/geometry/textures remain unchanged. The glTF meter convention does not verify real-world dimensions. Physical scale, mission-specific configuration, rigging, and mechanical operation are unverified. Unless explicitly controlled via the Ingenuity inspection MVP below, the renderer uses static poses.

chunks.title: SOURCES.md — Ingenuity mechanism & camera reference basis (MVP) (1/2)
chunks.text: Preserved project provenance at `/assets/provenance/ingenuity.csv` cites NASA technical sources (NASA Ingenuity Fact Sheet, NASA Rotor Geometry, NASA Landing Press Kit, and NASA Hover Modeling). The Ingenuity control specification (`src/config/deviceControlSpecs.ts`) distinguishes documented mission parameters from illustrative GLB inspection features:

chunks.title: SOURCES.md — Ingenuity mechanism & camera reference basis (MVP) (2/2)
chunks.text:
- **Documented NASA facts**: `1.8 kg` Earth mass (`~0.68 kg` Mars weight), `0.49 m` fuselage/mast height, coaxial counter-rotating `1.21 m` carbon-fiber rotors operating at `~2,400 rpm` for up to `~90 s` flights, `13.6 × 19.5 × 16.3 cm` avionics enclosure housing 6 Li-ion cells recharged via the top solar array, `RTE 13 MP` color horizon-facing camera, `Navcam 0.5 MP` grayscale nadir navigation camera + laser altimeter, and `~13 cm` underside ground clearance across 4 carbon composite landing legs.
- **GLB-verified structure**: `ingenuity_helicopter.glb` contains 11 named nodes (`bus`, `cams`, `leg_01`–`leg_04`, `parts_01`, `parts_02`, `rotors_01`, `rotors_02`, `solar_panel`). Node transforms verify `rotors_01` and `rotors_02` align their local `[1, 0, 0]` axes along opposite world vertical directions (`+Y` and `-Y`).
- **Illustrative / omitted scope**: All four camera presets (`overview`, `coaxial_mast`, `rte_horizon`, `navcam_nadir`) and the `0.5 rev/s` slow counter-rotation demo mode operate purely in normalized 2-unit GLB scene coordinates for structural visibility and are explicitly labeled illustrative (`isIllustrativeView: true`), not calibrated CAD frames or aerodynamic hover physics. Collective/cyclic blade pitch, landing-leg folding, battery charge, IMU state, and thermal telemetry are omitted because the GLB lacks separate hinge/pitch pivots and no measured flight telemetry dataset is integrated.

chunks.text:
- **Shared `TerrainProvider` & Deterministically Seeded Micro-Relief (`src/scene/terrain/terrainDataPipeline.ts`, `public/assets/terrain/manifest.json`)**:
  - Regional coordinates reference published landing areas: **Mars Ares Vallis** (`19.13°N, 326.78°E`, Mars Pathfinder baseline, gravity `3.72076 m/s²`, radius `3,389.5 km`) and **Moon Hadley–Apennine** (`26.1322°N, 3.6339°E`, Apollo 15 baseline, gravity `1.625 m/s²`, radius `1,737.4 km`).
  - Selectable exploration windows (`2×2 km`, `16×16 km`, `64×64 km`) stream `256×256 m` base tiles (`96×96` quads, `2.67 m` grid spacing, downsampled to LOD1 `32` & LOD2 `16` with downward skirts) plus spherical curvature drop (`computeSphericalDropM`) and dynamic `1 km` floating-origin rebasing.
  - **Honest disclosure (`isBaselinePlusSyntheticRelief: true`)**: Fine topographic undulations, craters, Hadley-style sinuous rille, basalt step slabs, and boulder fields are generated via deterministic seeded procedural math (`BODY_SEED`), **not** high-resolution raw HiRISE/LROC DTM rasters.

Static landers (`viking_lander`, `insight_lander`, `apollo_surface_pack`, `apollo_lm_mesa`) remain fixed by default and explicitly badge **`"Simulated mobility"`** when temporary educational roving is toggled on.

  - `SimulationClock` (`computeOrbitalTimeStep`) drives orbital actors and planet spin smoothly in both `ORBITAL_OVERVIEW` and orbital `CONTROL_ROOM_POV` cupola view (`1×..5000×` time-warp & pause), completely isolated from the fixed-60 Hz (`FIXED_PHYSICS_DT = 1/60`) surface Rapier simulation step.

# Mars–Moon Atlas: guided exploration implementation plan

Prepared 2026-11-14, Asia/Bangkok. Status: proposed implementation backlog, not completed features.

The intended outcome is a visitor who can ask a question, explore a place, inspect relevant equipment, explain one supported finding, and recognize what remains unknown. Use the existing Atlas and its shared scene to deliver that learning journey.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 3. Target journey and first release scope (1/2)
chunks.sourcePath: docs/EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md#3. Target journey and first release scope
chunks.section: 3. Target journey and first release scope
chunks.text:
1. **Choose a world and a question.** Show Mars and Moon, a one-sentence purpose, one recommended mission for each, and “Explore freely”. Avoid loading model fleets behind the invitation.
2. **Orient on the globe.** Start with a calm view, selected-world label, a clear illustration/data status, and one next action. An optional camera move is skippable and stops under reduced motion.
3. **Visit a story stop.** Show a title, a short “why this matters”, one question and a sourced position. Keep “Back to globe” and “View evidence” visible.
4. **Inspect evidence.** Offer the few relevant claims or layers. Missing coverage remains understandable; an unavailable dataset does not prevent reading the story.
5. **Connect to hardware.** Explain why this device or instrument is relevant to this place. Open the existing model inspector or a record with clearly labeled reconstruction status.
6. **Try a bounded activity.** Use an appropriate existing view/control. State whether the output is a documented fact, a calculated teaching example or an illustration.
7. **Reflect.** Present one finding, the source supporting it and one unanswered question. Offer a next mission, a copied deep link and local progress saving.

chunks.text:
The initial Mars candidate is a Jezero story connecting a scientific question to relevant Perseverance/Ingenuity observations. Exact relationships and claims must be reviewed before publication. Start the interactive exercise with the existing Ingenuity viewpoints: distinguish looking downward from looking toward the horizon, while identifying these camera placements as illustrative.

The initial Moon candidate uses Mare Tranquillitatis and Apollo 11 surface equipment/MESA, with a source-backed explanation of an observation or equipment task. Treat the existing procedural equipment as reconstruction. Do not attach Apollo 15/17 LRV operations to the Apollo 11 site. A later LRV story needs its own verified site/mission association and coordinates.

Each mission has a proposed 3–5 minute route with 3–4 stops. This is a design target, not measured completion time. Both routes must work as text and evidence cards if models or WebGL are unavailable. Free exploration preserves access to the broader reviewed catalog.

### P0 — Establish a stable and truthful baseline

chunks.text:
Baseline commands: `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run validate:assets`, `npm run build`, `npm run test:browser`. Extend browser assertions to inspect console shader errors as well as uncaught exceptions. Add a production-preview smoke check; the existing browser configuration starts the dev server.

The manifest now lists newly added Curiosity and Perseverance GLBs as available. Verify their files, hashes, sources and attribution; do not blindly revert them to the older checkpoint's “unavailable” description.

### P1 — Make the first minute clear

**Outcome:** a newcomer knows what to explore and how to proceed.

Add a small `MissionEntry` and `JourneyPanel` to the existing `App.tsx` shell. Add mission configuration rather than another scene. Update `CelestialQuickSelect.tsx` so the guided route prioritizes the current question and relevant destinations; move the full catalog behind an explicit “Explore freely” action. Hide orbital paths by default in guided mode while preserving the user's preference in free exploration.

Replace “Option 1 / Option 2” as primary labels with “Inspect model” and “Explore viewpoints”. Keep the mode details secondary. Replace asset-format labels such as “GLB + 8K” in primary navigation with descriptions of what visitors will see. Offer the full technical details in the evidence panel.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (4/11)
chunks.text:
On desktop, preserve the globe as the main visual area with one task panel and contextual details. On narrow screens, use a compact header, a useful globe viewport, and an accessible document-flow panel/drawer; avoid forcing visitors through a long equipment list to reach the story. Keep unavailable-layer explanations readable without hover.

Implement browser-history state through a URL adapter for validated body, mission, stop, target and view IDs. Example: `?v=1&body=mars&mission=jezero-evidence&stop=observe`. Unknown IDs return to a valid overview with a clear message. Back/forward restores a meaningful step. Camera drag, animation ticks and simulated telemetry do not create history entries.

**Gate:** five first-time participants attempt “choose a world, open a story stop, explain the image status” without coaching. Proposed target: at least four succeed within 60 seconds. Also verify keyboard traversal, 390 px layout, reduced motion and browser Back/Forward. This is a formative check, not a statistical claim.

### P2 — Make evidence inspectable at the claim level

**Outcome:** visitors can tell what a fact means, where it came from and what it does not establish.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (5/11)
chunks.text:
Introduce a source registry and reusable `EvidenceBadge`, `EvidenceCard` and `SourceDrawer`. Migrate `DossierMetric` beyond its current `{ label, value }` shape; its “Measured Mission Data” tab currently has no individual source/unit/date/method fields. Give narrative contributions claim references too. Preserve existing records during migration but do not promote unreviewed values to measured status.

Keep these three dimensions independent:

| Dimension | Proposed values | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evidence kind | measured, reported, derived, illustrative, unknown | How the claim or displayed value was produced |
| Representation | source model, procedural reconstruction, record only | What the visitor is viewing; a verified file does not verify physical fidelity |
| Runtime state | idle, loading, ready, error | Whether a resource loaded; this never upgrades its scientific status |

A claim records: stable ID, subject/mission, text or typed value, unit when applicable, source IDs, source locator, observation interval or publication date, version/check date, method and limitations. A derived value additionally records inputs and a reproducible method. Store uncertainty only when the source supplies it; otherwise say it is unspecified. “Unknown” data must not become zero.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (6/11)
chunks.text:
A layer also records: body, coverage, coordinate reference/projection, physical resolution when known, display resolution separately, date/version, source, attribution/terms and failure state. An 8K texture dimension is not a ground-resolution measurement. Only offer side-by-side quantitative comparison when units, coverage, coordinate frame and time context are compatible. Otherwise provide an explicitly qualitative comparison.

Render the same evidence component in POI stories, device dossiers and activity results. One action opens the relevant source and locator. Historical measurements stay visually separate from app-generated POV readouts.

**Gate:** every factual claim used in the two initial missions resolves to reviewed provenance. Every remaining dossier item has a source or a visible unverified status. Tests reject duplicate IDs, missing references, unsupported measured labels, invalid units/coordinates and incompatible layer comparisons. Retain original per-asset attribution.

### P3 — Connect stories, hardware and learning

**Outcome:** each interaction helps answer the visitor's question.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (7/11)
chunks.text:
Add `missionStories.ts` and a small relationship registry linking a story stop to a place, mission, instrument, evidence and capability. Each relationship carries its own source and role: deployed at, observed, regional context, flyby, or conceptual reference. Sharing a body ID is not proof of a relationship. Validate all references and prohibit accidental cross-mission links.

Reuse `DeviceModel`, `ProceduralDeviceModel`, `DeviceControlPanel`, `ControlRoomFirstPersonScene` and the current camera rig. Add capability metadata to `deviceControlSpecs.ts`: supported target, documented basis, illustrative/verified status, permitted inputs, output evidence type, reset behavior and limitations. A documented real-world mechanical limit is distinct from an interface yaw/pitch clamp.

Gate actions by capability. The current generic arm/boom and spectrometer buttons should not appear on every selected platform or POI. Retain supported camera inspection; label visual demos; omit unsupported actions. A simulated scan must never become a claimed composition measurement of the selected Mars/Moon site.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (8/11)
chunks.text:
Implement one complete Mars route first and record its acceptance evidence. Then implement the Moon route with the same story/evidence/activity components. Each stop offers a short narrative, optional deeper detail, an observation prompt and a clear next step. Add one reflection prompt that asks the visitor to distinguish observation from inference, rather than rewarding clicks or speed.

Add an `ExplorationNotebook` containing visited stops, selected evidence, one takeaway and an unknown. Save a small versioned record locally, with reset and storage-failure handling. Provide a deep link and plain-text summary export. Sharing remains optional; do not add an account requirement or automatic external transmission.

**Gate:** a visitor completes a short route for each body and explains one finding plus its limitation. Test evidence links, unsupported-action suppression, model failure recovery, rapid switching, local progress restoration and invalid/stale deep links. Closing or switching out of an activity stops its animation and releases obsolete resources.

### P4 — Add resilience, access and responsible context

**Outcome:** the same educational value remains available across devices and imperfect conditions.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (9/11)
chunks.text:
Accessibility starts in P1; this phase completes the audit. Target [WCAG 2.2 AA](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) with semantic navigation, visible focus, keyboard-operated tabs and drawers, text equivalents for meaningful canvas/POV information, and reduced motion covering auto-rotation and ongoing loops. The current POV overlay is entirely `aria-hidden`; retain decorative crosshairs as hidden but provide the meaningful state elsewhere. Use 44 CSS px as an internal touch-target goal, not as a statement of the AA minimum. Test zoom/reflow and screen-reader order manually as well as with automation.

Add a persistent low-data/text-first preference. Load mission text and sources first; defer high-resolution maps, fleet models and device GLBs until requested. Show download size before a large optional asset. Pause offscreen/hidden-tab work. Cache only bounded, versioned content with known redistribution terms. Offer a useful offline explanation and cached text where available; do not claim a full offline 3D mode without testing it.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (10/11)
chunks.text:
Measure startup bytes, time to usable text, time to first useful 3D view, frame time and renderer-resource counts on a named laptop and a real phone. Use cold/warm cache runs and the same camera/content before and after changes. Software WebGL checks are for functional coverage, not hardware performance claims. Provisional targets: usable text within 3 seconds under a documented 1.6 Mbps/150 ms test profile; no GLB or 8K map requests before opt-in in low-data mode; resource counts return near the documented warm baseline after ten body/activity switches. Revise these targets only with measured evidence.

Add one reviewed resilience exercise after P2/P3: for example, choose a useful observation when one explicitly modeled view is unavailable. Explain what changed and why the alternatives remain useful. If the numbers or physics are not validated, use a qualitative teaching exercise with stated assumptions.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 4. Delivery backlog (11/11)
chunks.text:
Add one optional stewardship/Earth-connection story when suitable evidence is ready. Separate analogy from demonstrated transfer, name the community/context, and cite any claimed benefit. Do not transplant a Low Earth Orbit debris score to Mars/Moon exploration. Do not invent a combined sustainability score. Broader hazard simulation, local/community content and numerical resource trade-offs remain separate later increments unless their inputs, method and validation are available.

**Gate:** the core journey works with keyboard, touch, reduced motion, WebGL unavailable and interrupted downloads. Users can tell a historical fact from simulated output. Each stewardship claim is sourced; each exercise states its assumptions and limits.

chunks.sourcePath: docs/EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md#5. Implementation seams and state ownership

| --- | --- |
| Rendering | Keep `MarsCanvas`, `CosmosSceneRoot`, existing body/model/terrain adapters and one camera rig. Story steps dispatch existing selection actions; they never mount a second scene. |

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 6. Sequence, effort and ownership (1/2)
chunks.text:
Estimates are planning ranges for one developer familiar with this codebase, with a science/content reviewer available. They are not calendar commitments. New terrain procurement, asset authoring, translations and unplanned shader/driver investigations are excluded.

| Increment | Dependencies | Developer effort | Review responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P0 baseline and critical truth corrections | Current tree inspection | 2–3 days | Engineering plus source/asset review |
| P1 guided entry, progressive disclosure, URL state | P0 status contract and stable rendering | 3–4 days | UX plus first-time visitor sessions |
| P2 claim evidence and content migration | P0 vocabulary; used by P1 shell | 3–5 days | Science/content reviewer |
| P3 Mars route, then Moon route, activities and notebook | P1 + reviewed P2 content | 4–6 days | Engineering, content and learning review |
| P4 access, bandwidth, resilience and one sourced context story | Core P3 journey; accessibility work starts in P1 | 3–5 days | QA, accessibility and content review |

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 6. Sequence, effort and ownership (2/2)
chunks.text: Full scope: roughly 15–23 developer-days plus review turnaround. Re-estimate after P0. If time is limited, ship P0, the P1 shell, P2 coverage for one mission and the Mars P3 route first; existing Moon free exploration remains available. Then reuse the verified route components for Moon. Do not trade source accuracy or accessibility for extra scenes.

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 7. Acceptance and release evidence (1/2)
chunks.text:
| Value | Proposed check |
| --- | --- |
| First-minute clarity | At least 4/5 formative participants choose a world, reach a story stop and identify content status within 60 seconds |
| Evidence literacy | At least 4/5 distinguish a sourced historical measurement from an illustrative view and open the supporting source without help |
| Learning | At least 4/5 give one correct takeaway and one limitation after a route; record the prompts and scoring rubric |
| Content integrity | All initial-route claims and relationships have reviewed sources; every displayed scientific value has a source or explicit unknown/unverified status |
| Recovery | Model 404, malformed GLB, decoder/texture failure, shader failure and context loss have recoverable outcomes; switching worlds stays usable |
| Navigation | Keyboard-only route, Back/Forward, direct links, refresh and local progress recovery pass; no focus traps or hidden focused controls |
| Access and performance | Verify text-first/low-data behavior, 390 px and 320 px layouts, 200% zoom, reduced motion and one physical phone; report measured timings and resource behavior |

chunks.title: EXPERIENCE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md — 7. Acceptance and release evidence (2/2)
chunks.text:
Extend existing Node tests and Playwright suites rather than creating a parallel framework. Browser coverage must collect console and page errors, exercise dev and production, include normal-motion and reduced-motion projects, and test Mars → Moon → Mars during active loading/POV sessions. Review screenshots for readability and content status, not merely pixel similarity.

For each completed increment, record changed files, reviewed claims/assets, exact validation commands/results, browser/device conditions and remaining limitations. The release gate is the current repository state passing its checks; old checkpoints do not satisfy it. Use the existing Vercel setup only when the actual target is configured and deployment is authorized. Missing deployment configuration does not block implementation or local verification.

Mission ID: jezero-evidence · Body: mars · Title: Jezero Journey: Searching for Traces of an Ancient Lake
Headline question: Why was Jezero Crater selected to search for evidence of ancient water on Mars?
Summary: Follow four stops, from the planetary overview and illustrative terrain to the Perseverance rover and Ingenuity helicopter.
Featured devices: perseverance_rover, ingenuity_helicopter, curiosity_rover · Featured POIs: jezero_crater, gale_crater
Stop 1 (observe): View Mars from Orbit — Where are Jezero and other notable features on the planetary globe? | What you see: An illustrative synthesized Mars globe at center, with markers leading to Jezero Crater. | Status note: Displays a synthesized illustrative globe (not quantitative real-time imagery).
Stop 2 (jezero): Jezero Terrain Mesh (Illustrative 3D) — How do the terrain relief and crater rim appear in the target area? | What you see: The illustrative Mars 3D terrain mesh can be rotated and zoomed to inspect the landforms. | Status note: Feature center from the IAU/USGS Gazetteer; the 3D terrain mesh is illustrative.
Stop 3 (investigate): Perseverance Rover — How do the optical assemblies, chassis, and robotic arm support rock and soil sample collection? | What you see: A size-normalized Perseverance 3D model with controls for selecting component groups. | Status note: NASA/JPL GLB model · Control-room operating values are illustrative simulations.
Stop 4 (compare): Ingenuity Helicopter — How did Ingenuity’s counter-rotating coaxial rotor design enable flight in the thin atmosphere? | What you see: The Ingenuity 3D model includes controls for inspecting components and stepping rotor rotation. | Status note: NASA/JPL GLB model · On-screen rotor motion uses an illustrative speed for visibility.

chunks.title: Apollo-Era Lunar Geology Survey (moon)
chunks.text:
Mission ID: hadley-geology · Body: moon · Title: Apollo-Era Lunar Geology Survey
Headline question: How do impact craters and Apollo rovers help reveal the Moon’s history?
Summary: Visit four stops, from dark basaltic maria to Tycho crater, the Apollo Lunar Module lander (NASA GLB), and an Apollo LRV 3D reconstruction.
Featured devices: apollo_lunar_module, apollo_lrv, apollo_surface_equipment · Featured POIs: mare_tranquillitatis, tycho, south_pole_aitken
Stop 1 (observe): View the Moon from Orbit — How do the dark basaltic maria differ from the bright, heavily cratered highlands? | What you see: An illustrative synthesized Moon globe at the center of the view, ready to guide you to Tycho crater. | Status note: Displays a synthesized illustrative globe (LOLA/Diviner measurement maps are not integrated).
Stop 2 (tycho): Tycho Crater Terrain Mesh (Illustrative) — What evidence of impact is shown by the crater-wall slope and surrounding area? | What you see: An illustrative lunar 3D terrain mesh in Inspect Model mode, which can be rotated to view its relief. | Status note: Feature center from the IAU/USGS Gazetteer; the 3D terrain mesh is for illustrative visualization.
Stop 3 (lrv): Apollo LRV (3D Reconstruction) — How did this foldable vehicle extend Apollo astronauts’ geological survey range? | What you see: An Apollo LRV 3D reconstruction with an option to switch to illustrative Explore Viewpoints mode. | Status note: Illustrative 3D reconstruction (the original Apollo LRV GLB is not integrated).
Stop 4 (lunar_module): Apollo Lunar Module Lander (NASA GLB) — How did the Lunar Module’s two-stage (Descent and Ascent Stage) design support landing on and launching from the Moon? | What you see: The normalized Apollo Lunar Module 3D model shows the two separate stages, four landing legs, and ascent module. | Status note: NASA Science 3D Resources GLB model · Static inspection only (no rig or real-scale collision).

chunks.title: VantaLumen guide: views and simulation shortcuts
chunks.text:
VantaLumen supports two exploration modes: "Guided journey" (the default, following Jezero/Hadley mission stops and temporarily hiding reference orbital paths) and "Explore freely" (showing the full catalog of equipment, features, orbits, and visual layers).
Two detailed view modes are available: "Inspect model" (MODEL_CLOSEUP — rotate a model normalized to a 2-unit longest side) and "Explore viewpoints" (CONTROL_ROOM_POV — control-room or field perspective on 3D terrain or in orbit).
Explore Viewpoints shortcuts: use WASD or the arrow keys to drive a rover or fly the Ingenuity helicopter (Q/Space to increase throttle or ascend, E/Shift to descend with the helicopter), C to switch between First Person (Mastcam/Eye) and Chase views, and R to restore the equipment pose.
Terrain simulation offers three area sizes (2×2 km, 16×16 km, 64×64 km) and four graphics quality levels (Auto, Low, Medium, High). Terrain and surface textures are illustrative simulations generated from mathematical seeds and reference coordinates for Ares Vallis and Hadley–Apennine; they are not measured HiRISE/LROC DEM maps.
Shareable URLs use the format ?v=1&body=mars|moon&mission=...&stop=... or &mode=free&target=...&view=overview|inspect|viewpoints. The system cross-checks body/mission/target to prevent mismatches.
